Kind of like developing arts if there is no direct crisis

That tension is real, and it touches on how we value human experience.

When a trait directly solves problems—turning chaos into order, building systems, securing resources—it carries immediate evolutionary and social feedback. Because society actively rewards those practical competencies, the ego naturally latches onto them. It feels safe to double down on what works, so we optimize our problem-solving faculties, analytical power, and functional strengths.

The issue arises when utility becomes the only metric of worth.

When every hour has to produce an outcome, non-utilitarian pursuits get sidelined as "luxuries" or "inefficiencies." But arts, music, play, and unquantifiable exploration aren't just decorative add-ons reserved for when all problems are permanently solved—they are how we process meaning, connect with our senses, and prevent life from collapsing into a perpetual maintenance loop. If you only ever build the scaffolding and never inhabit the space inside, the utility loses its entire purpose.

Developing the non-instrumental parts of yourself—the crafts, music, or aesthetic experiments that don't need an ROI—actually balances out that rigid optimization. It gives you a way to exist without constantly having to prove competence or conquer chaos.

What prompted this thought today—have you been feeling the pull to give more room to something purely expressive?

It's not as stable as it looks. It's very dependent on things Developing skills that don't have any roi right now. turns.response_html:
Treating ROI as your primary operating system makes your identity hostage to external conditions. When your self-worth and purpose are tied strictly to utility, output, and leverage, you’re only as stable as the market, the problem in front of you, or your current capacity to execute. It feels like control, but it's actually fragile because it requires a continuous stream of problems to conquer to justify itself.

The idea of practicing something to "untrain and forget" gets to the heart of what genuine rest and non-utilitarian craft actually do:

  • Breaking the instrumental loop: In problem-solving mode, every action is a means to an end. An activity with no expected return forces you into the present tense—you have to inhabit the tactile, immediate reality of what you're doing rather than mentally living three steps ahead in the finished product.
  • Unclenching the analytical mind: When there is no scoreboard, efficiency metric, or deliverable, the brain's executive control network gets to stand down. It unlearns the habit of treating every input as data to be optimized.
  • Building an anchor outside the ego: Engaging in something where you aren't trying to be "good," fast, or productive builds a core of self-trust that doesn't depend on competence or validation.

It turns non-productive pursuits from an inefficient distraction into an essential pressure release. You aren't doing it to become better at your work; you're doing it to remember who is doing the living beneath the work.

turns.response_html:
When the economic filter becomes the sole lens for self-worth, it crowds out every other ecosystem of meaning. It acts like an invasive species in your mental ecology—optimizing for a single, easily quantifiable metric while starving everything that can't be put on a ledger.

Historically, human value was diversified across multiple pillars:

  • Relational and communal: Being a reliable neighbor, a good sibling, a steward of a shared space, or a solid presence in a group.
  • Craft and physical stewardship: Taking care of living things, working with physical materials, or making something with your hands simply to see it exist well.
  • Interior and expressive: Engaging with music, physical movement, contemplation, or philosophy where the experience is the reward, not a milestone to check off.

When you monocrop your identity around utility, leverage, and economic heuristics, you become extremely vulnerable. The moment the market shifts, a project ends, or your energy dips, the whole framework wobbles because there are no other roots holding the soil together.

Worse, you atrophy in the exact domains that make an actual life worth living—spontaneity, sensory appreciation, patience, and uncalculated human connection. Those capacities require you to operate without a stopwatch or an optimization function.

Letting off the gas isn't falling behind; it's diversifying your sources of meaning so a dip in one area doesn't bankrupt your entire sense of self.
